title: Leaders Who Hide Behind Their Intentions Dont Apologize Often Enough
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article confronts a common leadership avoidance pattern: excusing hurtful behavior by pointing to good intentions instead of offering a genuine apology. It argues that many leaders treat apologizing as a sign of weakness and so default to explaining away their mistakes, leaving colleagues uncertain about where they stand. The piece frames a sincere apology as an act of accountability and strength rather than vulnerability, and challenges readers to reflect honestly on how recently they have actually apologized to someone at work.
points: Leaders often excuse hurtful behavior by citing good intentions instead of offering a genuine apology.
Many leaders wrongly treat apologizing as a sign of weakness rather than strength.
Failing to apologize leaves colleagues uncertain about the relationship and whether the behavior will recur.
Good intentions do not exempt a leader from acknowledging the actual impact of their actions.
A sincere apology signals accountability and reinforces relational trust rather than undermining authority.
quotes: Too many leaders hide behind their intentions and fail to apologize for their misdeeds.
Many leaders view mistakes and the apologies that follow them as signs of weakness.
Simply believing that they didn’t intend to do harm, insult, or offense doesn’t allow a leader to explain away the transgression.
By admitting to and taking full ownership of your mistakes, you show yourself to be human, not weak.
The symbolism of saying you’re sorry goes well beyond the present moment. It is a powerful reflection of how a leader relates to the truth.
